newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Welteke - EMU benefits should be emphasised.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Welteke - EMU benefits should be emphasised.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said on Saturday not enough was being done to stress the advantages of European economic and monetary union and that public debate focused too much on fears the Euro may be weak.
Welteke said economic convergence among European nations on inflation, exchange rates and interest rates had been stronger than expected.

While the debate appeared to have been narrowed down to who met the convergence criteria on public debt and the budget deficit, the Maastricht Treaty did not automatically exclude nations from monetary union if they exceeded the limits set.

For example, Belgium was likely to join monetary union even though its public debt far exceeded the 60 percent of GDP limit laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, Welteke told a conference of Social Democrats in Hattersheim near Frankfurt.
"Amid all the debate about Maastricht we must not forget that price stability, exchange rates and interest rates give an excellent picture in the majority of European Union countries.
"It is time to go on the offensive in discussing the advantages of European Union and not to spread fear of a weak currency," Welteke said.
Welteke, a member of the Social Democrat party, is president of the state central bank of Hesse.

Countries seeking to qualify for monetary union, scheduled to be launched in 1999, should aim to be within levels targeted by the Maastricht Treaty for public debt, budget deficit, inflation, exchange rates and interest rates.

The European Monetary Institute, forerunner of the European Central Bank, warned on Wednesday that most EU states did not yet make the grade for monetary union and were dragging their heels on getting their finances in order.
Welteke said the Euro would create exchange rate stability and thereby benefit the economy.
Extreme swings in exchange rates tended to weaken productivity and the mark's role as a world reserve currency had been a burden on the Germany economy in the past, he said.
Welteke warned that a failure of monetary union could cause a return to nationalism and regionalism.
But he said price stability could be at risk if too many candidates were allowed to sign up to the Euro from the start or if some monetary union members failed to maintain fiscal discipline.
